en: Buddhavamsa 16:
The Lineage of Buddha Atthadassī “In that very same aeon of adornment (maṇḍakappa),” [it is said].
Atthadassī, of great renown,
having destroyed the great darkness,
attained supreme enlightenment.
Being entreated by Brahmā,
the Sage set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma;
he satisfied the world with the Deathless.
The realm of the Dasasahassiya devas.
For that Lord of the World as well,
there were three moments of clear comprehension.
When the Buddha Atthadassī appeared, there was the first realization for one hundred thousand times ten million beings.
He practiced the divine course;
there was a second realization for hundreds of thousands of millions.
Furthermore, when the Buddha taught in the presence of his father to one hundred thousand koṭis,
The third realization occurred.
There were three assemblies for that Great Seer as well.
Of those whose taints were exhausted, who were stainless,
whose minds were peaceful, and who were poised—
of eighty-nine thousand such ones.
The first assembly took place;
the second assembly consisted of eighty-eight thousand.
The third assembly consisted of one hundred and seventy-eight thousand [monks],
all liberated through non-clinging.
Of those stainless Great Seers.
At that time,
I was a matted-hair ascetic practicing fierce austerities.
Susīma by name,
esteemed as the best on earth,
[offered] a divine mandārava flower.
Having brought a lotus and a pāricchattaka tree from the world of the gods,
I made offerings to the Perfectly Awakened One.
The Buddha Atthadassī, the Great Sage, also prophesied of me:
"In eighteen hundred aeons..."
"This one will become a Buddha.
Having exerted himself in striving... [and so forth].
"We shall do this in his presence.
Having heard her words as well,
he was joyful and his mind was filled with spiritual urgency.
I resolved upon a further vow for the fulfillment of the ten perfections.
There was a city named Sobhana.
The kṣatriya named Sāgara was the father,
and the mother named Sudassanā was the birth-giver of the Teacher Atthadassi.
For ten thousand years he lived the household life;
Amaragiri was his excellent mountain chariot.
There were three supreme palaces and thirty-three thousand women beautifully adorned.
There was a woman named Visākhā,
and her son was named Sela.
Having seen four omens,
He went forth by means of a single horse;
for no less than eight months,
the Victor exerted himself in striving.
Being entreated by Brahmā, the virtuous and highly renowned Atthadassī,
the Great Hero, set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion.
In the Anoma monastery, the Bull among Men had two chief disciples who were holy and serene.
Abhaya was the attendant of the Teacher Atthadassi;
and there were also Dhamma and Sudhamma.
were his chief female disciples;
the Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called the Campaka.
Nakula and Nisabha were the chief attendants,
as were Makila and Sunanda.
They were his foremost attendants.
That Buddha too was peerless and equal to the Unequaled,
rising eighty cubits high.
He shines like the king of sāl trees,
like the full moon;
his natural rays of light—
Numbering many hundreds of millions,
they constantly pervade ten yojanas above, below, and in the ten directions.
He too was a Buddha, a bull among men,
the Sage supreme over all beings,
for a hundred thousand years.
The One with Vision stood in the world,
having displayed incomparable radiance and shone forth throughout the realm of gods.
He too has reached impermanence,
through the destruction of grasping at the highest state;
thus [spoke] Atthadassī, the supreme Victor.
He attained Nibbāna at Anomārāma;
his relics were distributed throughout various regions.
The fourteenth lineage is that of the Blessed One Atthadassī.
